17447: It shows the same pattern as Isaiah 44-45 from Babylon's side: a god choosing Cyrus. Marduk gets the credit here, Yahweh in Isaiah. Its policy of restoring peoples and temples fits the decree in Ezra, though the cylinder does not mention Jews. It also shows that Bel (Marduk) was honoured, not humiliated, when Babylon fell, which bears on how Isa 46:1-2 is read.
17450: Sennacherib's South-West Palace, Nineveh; now in the British Museum
17451: Found during Austen Henry Layard's excavations at Nineveh in the late 1840s, these carved stone panels show Assyria's siege of the Judahite city of Lachish in 701 BC: siege ramps, battering rams, impaled prisoners, families deported, and soldiers carrying away booty, including objects many read as cult equipment such as large incense stands.
17452: The reliefs confirm the campaign described in Kings and illustrate the Assyrian claim, voiced by the Rabshakeh, that no nation's gods had saved it. Assyrian armies usually carried off the statues of defeated gods; some scholars note that no divine image appears among Lachish's spoils, which may fit Judah's largely aniconic worship of Yahweh, though this argument from silence is debated.
17454: Tell Deir Alla, Jordan Valley, Jordan
17455: A Dutch team led by Henk Franken found fragments of a plaster wall text written in red and black ink in 1967. It opens with 'the account of Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods'. The gods come to him at night; he weeps and tells how the gods and the 'shaddayin' met in assembly and ordered a goddess to close the heavens, bringing darkness and disaster.
17456: It is the only extra-biblical text naming a biblical prophet from this region and period, and shows that Balaam was remembered east of the Jordan as a famous seer, matching Numbers 22-24. Its 'shaddayin' and divine assembly connect with the Bible's title Shaddai and with the idea of a council of gods. Its language (Aramaic, Canaanite or a local dialect) is debated.
17458: Ketef Hinnom, above the Hinnom Valley, Jerusalem
17459: Gabriel Barkay found two tiny rolled silver amulets in a burial cave in 1979. When unrolled they contained a blessing close to the priestly blessing of Numbers 6: 'May YHWH bless you and keep you; may YHWH make his face shine on you and give you peace'. A 2004 re-study with new imaging confirmed the late Iron Age date.
17460: They are the oldest known texts with wording found in the Bible, and they come from the very valley where Topheth stood. Only YHWH is invoked, a useful contrast to the 'YHWH and his asherah' blessings, showing the range of Judahite religion around Josiah's time.
17461: Zeus and Hermes inscriptions near Lystra
17463: Sedasa and the region of Lystra, Lycaonia (south-central Turkey)
17464: Inscriptions published by the classicist W. M. Calder in the early 20th century record the dedication to Zeus of a statue of Hermes by local men with Lycaonian names, and an altar to Zeus 'who hears prayer' and Hermes. The exact discovery dates and readings should be checked against the published editions.
17465: Though later than Paul, they show Zeus and Hermes worshipped together in this very district, as Acts 14 assumes, and fit the local legend (told by Ovid) of the two gods visiting the region in human form.
17467: c. 560 BC; rebuilt after 356 BC; destroyed AD 262
17469: After years of searching, the engineer John Turtle Wood found the site of the temple on 31 December 1869. One of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, the temple was rebuilt on a huge scale after a fire in 356 BC. Wood also found, in the theatre, the Salutaris inscription (AD 104) describing processions of gold and silver images of Artemis through the city. Statues of Ephesian Artemis, with distinctive rows of bulbous shapes on her chest, were later found in the city.
17470: The finds illustrate Acts 19: a city proud to be 'temple guardian' of Artemis, a trade in her images, a vast theatre, and an image said to have 'fallen from heaven'. They show what was at stake economically and civically when the goddess lost worshippers.
17471: Elephantine papyri: the Yahu temple and Anat-Yahu
17474: Aramaic papyri began reaching collectors in 1893 and further finds came from excavations in 1906-08. They come from a Jewish military colony that had a temple to YHW (Yahu) on the island. Letters describe its destruction in 410 BC by priests of the local god Khnum, and a petition (407 BC) to the Persian governor of Judah and to the sons of Sanballat for permission to rebuild. A temple collection list records money for YHW, Eshem-bethel and Anat-bethel, and an oath names Anat-Yahu.
17475: These Jews offered sacrifice to Yahweh outside Jerusalem and apparently honoured other deities alongside him, about a century after Jeremiah confronted Judahites in Egypt. Whether Anat-Yahu was a goddess treated as Yahweh's consort or an aspect of Yahweh is debated. The papyri also name Sanballat, the opponent of Nehemiah.
17476: Temple vessels for Baal, Asherah and the host of heaven
17477: Hilkiah and the priests bring out of Yahweh's temple all the vessels made for Baal, Asherah and the host of heaven. Josiah burns them outside Jerusalem in the fields of the Kidron and carries the ashes to Bethel, the northern shrine he will later defile.
17479: He removes the kemarim, priests appointed by Judah's kings to burn incense at the high places to Baal, the sun, the moon, the constellations (mazzalot, perhaps the zodiac) and all the host of heaven.
17480: The Asherah image in the temple
17481: He brings the Asherah (the image Manasseh had placed in the temple, 2 Kgs 21:7) out to the Kidron, burns it, grinds it to dust and throws the dust on the graves of the common people.
17482: Houses of the qedeshim and the weavers for Asherah
17483: He breaks down the houses of the qedeshim (often translated 'male cult prostitutes', though their role is debated) in the temple, where women wove hangings (or garments) for Asherah.
17484: High places from Geba to Beersheba
17485: He brings the priests from the towns of Judah to Jerusalem and defiles the high places where they burned incense, from Geba in the north to Beersheba in the south. These were mostly local shrines to Yahweh, now banned in favour of the one temple.
17487: He breaks down the high places at the city gate of Joshua the governor. Some scholars emend 'gates' (she'arim) to 'goat-demons' (se'irim), compare Lev 17:7.
17489: The former high-place priests may not serve at Yahweh's altar in Jerusalem, though they eat unleavened bread among their fellow priests.
17490: Topheth in the Valley of Hinnom
17491: He defiles Topheth in the Valley of the son of Hinnom so that no one can make a son or daughter pass through fire to Molech.
17492: Horses and chariots of the sun
17493: He removes the horses the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun at the entrance of the temple, by the chamber of Nathan-melech, and burns the chariots of the sun.
17495: He pulls down the altars on the roof of Ahaz's upper room (likely for astral worship, compare Jer 19:13; Zeph 1:5) and the altars Manasseh built in the two temple courts, smashes them and throws the dust into the Kidron.
17496: Solomon's shrines on the Mount of Corruption
17497: He defiles the high places east of Jerusalem, south of the Mount of Corruption, that Solomon built for Ashtoreth of the Sidonians, Chemosh of Moab and Milcom of the Ammonites.
17498: Pillars and Asherim broken, bones scattered
17499: He breaks the standing stones, cuts down the Asherim (sacred poles) and fills their places with human bones, making them permanently unclean.
17501: He tears down the altar and high place Jeroboam built at Bethel, burns the high place, grinds it to dust and burns the Asherah there.
17502: Bones burned on the Bethel altar
17503: Seeing tombs on the hillside, he takes the bones and burns them on the altar, fulfilling the word of the man of God from Judah (1 Kgs 13:2).
17505: He leaves untouched the grave of the man of God who predicted this, and the bones of the old prophet from Samaria buried with him.
17506: Shrines in the cities of Samaria
17507: He removes all the houses of the high places in the towns of Samaria that the kings of Israel had built, doing to them as he did at Bethel.
17509: He kills the priests of the high places there on their altars and burns human bones on them, then returns to Jerusalem. This is harsher than his treatment of Judah's priests (2 Kgs 23:9).
17510: Mediums, spiritists, teraphim and idols (after the Passover)
17511: Just beyond the main list, he also removes mediums, necromancers, household gods (teraphim), idols (gillulim) and all the abominations in Judah and Jerusalem, to carry out the words of the book found in the temple.
17514: In the older biblical texts the gods of other nations are treated as real powers tied to their own lands. Jephthah can say to the Ammonites, 'Will you not possess what Chemosh your god gives you?'; David, driven out of Israel, complains he is being told to 'go, serve other gods'; Naaman takes Israelite soil home so he can worship Yahweh in Syria. Deut 32:8-9 pictures the nations allotted to heavenly beings while Israel is Yahweh's own portion. The point is not that these gods equal Yahweh, but that they are rivals in a crowded heavenly world.
17516: the 'god of the land' in Samaria
17517: Prophetic mockery: gods as man-made things
17519: The prophets push further: idols are wood, stone and metal made by tired workmen, carried on animals, nailed down so they will not fall over. They cannot speak, walk or save. In this phase the focus is on the emptiness of the image, and in Second Isaiah the claim becomes that there is no other god at all.
17520: half a log for cooking, half for a god (Isa 44)
17521: a scarecrow in a cucumber field (Jer 10:5)
17522: Bel and Nebo as heavy baggage (Isa 46)
17526: A few Hebrew texts take a different line: behind the idols stand real spiritual beings, but lesser and harmful ones. Moses' Song says Israel sacrificed 'to shedim, not God, to gods they had not known'; Ps 106 says they sacrificed their sons and daughters to the shedim. The word is related to Akkadian shedu, a protective spirit. Other texts mention se'irim, 'goat-demons', to whom sacrifices were forbidden.
17530: The Septuagint: the gods become daimonia
17532: When Jewish scholars in Alexandria translated the Scriptures into Greek, they often used daimonia (demons) for foreign gods. Ps 96:5 ('all the gods of the nations are nothings') became 'all the gods of the nations are demons'; Deut 32:17 became 'they sacrificed to demons and not to God'; Isa 65:3 adds that Israel burned incense 'to demons, which do not exist'. In Greek, daimon had been a neutral word for a divine being; this translation helped turn it into a word for evil spirits.
17533: Ps 95:5 LXX (= Ps 96:5): 'the gods of the nations are daimonia'
17535: Baruch 4:7 (Apocrypha): 'sacrificing to demons and not to God'
17536: Second Temple writings: Watchers and evil spirits
17538: Jewish writings outside the Hebrew canon give the demons a back-story. In 1 Enoch's Book of the Watchers, rebel angels (the 'sons of God' of Gen 6) descend on Mount Hermon, teach forbidden arts and father giants; when the giants die their spirits become evil spirits that afflict humanity (1 Enoch 15:8-12), and the angels' spirits lead people to sacrifice to demons as to gods (1 Enoch 19:1). Jubilees has Mastema, chief of the spirits, keep a tenth of them to lead people into error and idolatry (Jubilees 10-11). These books are not part of most canons (1 Enoch and Jubilees are canonical in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church) but were widely read when the New Testament was written.
17540: 1 Enoch 19:1 (spirits lead people to sacrifice to demons)
17542: Dead Sea Scrolls songs against demons
17543: New Testament: idols nothing, demons real
17545: Paul holds both strands together: an idol is nothing and there is one God and one Lord (1 Cor 8:4-6), yet what pagans sacrifice they offer 'to demons and not to God', echoing Deut 32:17 in its Greek form, so Christians cannot share the Lord's table and the table of demons. The Gospels speak of Beelzebul, a Philistine Baal-title, as 'prince of demons'. In Philippi Paul expels a 'Python spirit' from a slave girl, linking a Greek oracle (Apollo's Pythian prophecy) to demonic power. Revelation lists worship of demons and idols together.
17549: 'those that by nature are not gods' (Gal 4:8)
17550: Church fathers: the pagan gods were demons
17552: Early Christian apologists made this the standard explanation of paganism. Justin Martyr argued that evil demons, offspring of the fallen angels, had passed themselves off as the gods of Greek myth and persecuted Socrates and Christians alike (*First Apology* 5; *Second Apology* 5). Tertullian challenged magistrates to bring someone possessed before a tribunal and watch the 'god' confess it was a demon when ordered by a Christian (*Apology* 22-23). Augustine devoted much of *City of God* (books 8-10) to showing that the gods honoured by Rome were demons seeking worship.
17559: Jerome's Latin Vulgate spelled the Gospels' Beelzebul as 'Beelzebub', and Western tradition made him a prince of hell. Later demonologies and magical handbooks ranked the old gods as officers in an infernal hierarchy: Astarte became Astaroth, now a male 'great duke' of hell; Baal became Bael, a demon king; Baal-peor became Belphegor. Lists of this kind appear in Johann Weyer's *Pseudomonarchia daemonum* (1577) and the 17th-century *Lesser Key of Solomon*, and were popularised in Collin de Plancy's *Dictionnaire infernal* (1818).
17561: Astaroth, duke of hell (a goddess turned male)
17565: Milton's *Paradise Lost* (1667): the catalogue of fallen angels
17567: In Book 1 of *Paradise Lost* John Milton gives a roll-call of fallen angels who later, he says, would be worshipped as gods by the nations. Beelzebub is Satan's second in command. The list follows the Old Testament closely: Moloch, smeared with the blood of child sacrifice; Chemos (Chemosh) with Peor; the Baalim and Ashtaroth; Astoreth the moon-goddess of Sidon; Thammuz mourned by the women of Zion; Dagon, who grieved when the captured ark maimed his image; Rimmon of Damascus; Egypt's Osiris, Isis and Orus; and Belial. Through Milton the Bible's rival gods passed into English literature as named devils.
